title: Who is the “captain of the host of the Lord” that Joshua meets by Jericho?
summary: By Jericho Joshua sees “a man” with a drawn sword who calls himself “captain of the host of the Lord”. Joshua falls on his face and is told to take off his shoe because the place is holy. The passage does not say who or what this figure is, and he delivers no message in the three verses that tell of him.
text: KJV Joshua 5:13: “behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand: and Joshua went unto him, and said unto him, Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” KJV 5:14: “And he said, Nay; but as captain of the host of the Lord am I now come. And Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship, and said unto him, What saith my Lord unto his servant?” KJV 5:15: “And the captain of the Lord's host said unto Joshua, Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy. And Joshua did so.” KJV 6:1: “Now Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel” KJV 6:2: “And the Lord said unto Joshua, See, I have given into thine hand Jericho” KJV Exodus 3:5: “put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” KJV Genesis 23:7: “And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land” KJV Revelation 22:8: “I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things” KJV Revelation 22:9: “Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 5:13: וְהִנֵּה־אִישׁ֙ עֹמֵ֣ד לְנֶגְדֹּ֔ו [and behold a man standing over against him]. 5:14: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ׀ לֹ֗א כִּ֛י אֲנִ֥י שַׂר־צְבָֽא־יְהוָ֖ה עַתָּ֣ה בָ֑אתִי [and he said, No; for I am the captain of the host of the LORD; now I have come]; וַיִּשְׁתָּ֔חוּ [and he bowed down]. 5:15: שַׁל־נַֽעַלְךָ֙ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֔ךָ [loose thy sandal from off thy foot]. Exodus 3:5: שַׁל־נְעָלֶ֙יךָ֙ מֵעַ֣ל רַגְלֶ֔יךָ [loose thy sandals from off thy feet]. Genesis 23:7: וַיִּשְׁתַּ֥חוּ לְעַם־הָאָ֖רֶץ [and he bowed down to the people of the land]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 5:14: ἐγὼ ἀρχιστράτηγος δυνάμεως Κυρίου, νυνὶ παραγέγονα. Καὶ Ἰησοῦς ἔπεσεν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ, δέσποτα, τί προστάσσεις τῷ σῷ οἰκέτῃ; [I, chief captain of the force of the Lord, have now come. And Joshua fell on his face upon the earth and said to him, Master, what dost thou command thy servant?]. Greek New Testament (TISCH) Revelation 22:9: τῷ θεῷ προσκύνησον [worship God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/3/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/23/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/66/22/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/66/22/.
reasoning: The figure is first called “a man”, then gives himself a title found in the KJV only in these two verses, and Joshua answers by falling on his face and calling him “my Lord”. Whether Joshua is meeting a human officer, an angel or God bears on what Joshua’s act is and on who speaks next: the three verses give no message from the captain beyond the command about the shoe, and the next words of instruction are introduced with “And the Lord said unto Joshua” after a verse about Jericho being shut up.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the captain is an angel who commands the heavenly armies; that he is the Lord appearing in the form of a man, so that Joshua 6:2 continues the same meeting, a reading that points to the words about holy ground said to Moses at Exodus 3:5; that he is Christ before his birth, a reading held by some Christian interpreters. Limits on each: the Hebrew verb the KJV renders “did worship” here is the verb it renders “bowed himself” at Genesis 23:7, where it is done to men, so the verb alone does not show that the one bowed to is God, and a shared verb does not settle context; Revelation 22:8–9 has an angel refuse worship, which is quoted as a text used in this debate and not as an answer about Joshua; the passage does not say that the speaker of 6:2 is the captain. Brenton’s Greek of 5:14 as quoted has no word for “Nay” and no clause for “and did worship”; that difference is noted and not examined here. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “captain of the host of the Lord” and “captain of the Lord's host” finds Joshua 5:14 and 5:15 only; a search for “prince of the host” finds Daniel 8:11, which was not examined; Joshua 5:13–6:2 was read in the KJV. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle who the captain is. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: Rahab’s house was “upon the town wall” — how were the spies sent into it after “the wall fell down flat”?
summary: Rahab’s house is said to be upon the wall of Jericho, and her family is to be kept safe by staying inside it. The account then says the wall “fell down flat”, and afterwards Joshua sends the two spies into her house to bring the family out. The verses compared do not say how the house was still there to be entered.
text: KJV Joshua 2:15: “Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall.” KJV 2:18: “thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by” KJV 2:19: “whosoever shall be with thee in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand be upon him” KJV 6:5: “the wall of the city shall fall down flat, and the people shall ascend up every man straight before him” KJV 6:17: “only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house” KJV 6:20: “the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city” KJV 6:22: “But Joshua had said unto the two men that had spied out the country, Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath, as ye sware unto her.” KJV 6:23: “And the young men that were spies went in, and brought out Rahab” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 2:15: כִּ֤י בֵיתָהּ֙ בְּקִ֣יר הַֽחֹומָ֔ה וּבַֽחֹומָ֖ה הִ֥יא יֹושָֽׁבֶת [for her house was in the side of the wall, and in the wall she was dwelling]. 6:20: וַתִּפֹּ֨ל הַֽחֹומָ֜ה תַּחְתֶּ֗יהָ [and the wall fell in its place]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 2:15, the whole verse as printed: Καὶ κατεχάλασεν αὐτοὺς διὰ τῆς θυρίδος [and she let them down through the window]. 6:20: καὶ ἔπεσεν ἅπαν τὸ τεῖχος κύκλῳ [and all the wall fell round about]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/6/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS06.htm.
reasoning: The agreement with Rahab depends on the house: her family must be inside it, and the window in the wall is to be marked. The fall of the wall is then told without any exception, and the next thing said of the house is that the spies are sent into it and bring the family out. Whether the house stood, and so whether the whole wall fell or a part of it, changes how “the wall fell down flat” is to be read, and the verses compared do not say.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses state: that the stretch of wall with her house was left standing; that the wall fell where the people stood and went up “every man straight before him”, and not on every side; that the house was built against the side of the wall, as the Hebrew wording quoted can be taken, and was not brought down with it; that the account is brief and passes over how the family came through. The record does not say the two statements cannot both be true. In Brenton’s Greek the wording differs at both ends: 2:15 as printed has no clause about the house or the wall, and the 24 verses printed on the cited page for chapter 2 were searched for the Greek word for wall and it was not found; 6:20 says “all the wall fell round about”. Those differences are noted and no G is proposed here. Check made: Joshua 2:15–21, 6:1, 6:5, 6:15–17 and 6:20–25 were read in the KJV; a search of the packaged KJV for “Rahab” and “Rachab” finds, outside Joshua, Matthew 1:5, Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 of this woman and three verses of the Psalms and Isaiah that use the name otherwise, and none of those speaks of her house or the wall. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle how the house was standing. A published record cites some of these verses on the extent of the conquest; this record asks only about the house and the wall. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: What was “the book of Jasher”, and how much of the sun-and-moon passage is taken from it?
summary: In the middle of the account of the sun standing still the text asks, “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” The same book is named once more, at David’s lament. Neither place says what the book was, and Joshua does not mark which of the words around the question are quoted from it.
text: KJV Joshua 10:12: “and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.” KJV 10:13: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.” KJV 10:14: “And there was no day like that before it or after it” KJV 2 Samuel 1:17: “And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son:” KJV 2 Samuel 1:18: “(Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.)” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 10:13: הֲלֹא־הִ֥יא כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֣פֶר הַיָּשָׁ֑ר [is it not written upon the book of the upright]. 2 Samuel 1:18: הִנֵּ֥ה כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֥פֶר הַיָּשָֽׁר [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 10:13: Καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἐν στάσει, ἕως ἠμύνατο ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς αὐτῶν· καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος κατὰ μέσον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [and the sun stood and the moon in their station until God avenged himself on their enemies; and the sun stood in the middle of heaven]. 2 Samuel 1:18: ἰδοὺ γέγραπται ἐπὶ βιβλίου τοῦ εὐθοῦς [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS10.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA01.htm.
reasoning: The question about the book stands between two statements that the sun stood still. If the words before it, or the words on both sides of it, are taken from a book of songs, the standing of the sun is being reported in that book’s words; if only the narrator is speaking, it is told as plain narrative. The passage names the book and does not say what kind of book it was, who wrote it, or where the words taken from it begin and end.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the book was a collection of songs, since the other thing said to be written in it is David’s lament; that “Jasher” is not a person’s name and the title means “the book of the upright”, as the Hebrew and the Greek of 2 Samuel 1:18 can be rendered; that only the address to the sun and moon and the lines before the question are from the book, with the words after it being the narrator’s own; that the words after the question are from the book as well. None of these readings by itself decides whether the event is told as literal or as figure. Brenton’s Greek of Joshua 10:13 as quoted runs from the first statement to the second with no sentence about a book between them, and the 41 verses printed on the cited page for chapter 10 were searched for the Greek word for book and it was not found; that difference is noted and no G is proposed here. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “Jasher” finds Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18 only; Joshua 10:12–14 and 2 Samuel 1:17–18 were read in the KJV. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the book was or how much is quoted from it. A published record sets a literal reading of the long day beside astronomy, and another asks about a different book named at Numbers 21:14; this record asks only about the book named here. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God” — which words, and in which book?
summary: After the covenant at Shechem, Joshua is said to have written “these words in the book of the law of God”. The verse does not say which words he wrote, or whether the book is the book of the law that Moses wrote and had placed beside the ark, which the book of Joshua elsewhere calls “the book of the law of Moses”.
text: KJV Joshua 24:25: “So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.” KJV 24:26: “And Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God, and took a great stone, and set it up there under an oak, that was by the sanctuary of the Lord.” KJV 24:27: “for it hath heard all the words of the Lord which he spake unto us” KJV 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth” KJV 8:31: “as it is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV 23:6: “all that is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV Deuteronomy 31:24: “And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,” KJV Deuteronomy 31:26: “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 24:26: וַיִּכְתֹּ֤ב יְהֹושֻׁ֙עַ֙ אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה בְּסֵ֖פֶר תֹּורַ֣ת אֱלֹהִ֑ים [and Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God]. 8:31: כַּכָּתוּב֙ בְּסֵ֙פֶר֙ תֹּורַ֣ת מֹשֶׁ֔ה [as it is written in the book of the law of Moses]. Deuteronomy 31:24: לִכְתֹּ֛ב אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֥י הַתֹּורָֽה־הַזֹּ֖את עַל־סֵ֑פֶר עַ֖ד תֻּמָּֽם [to write the words of this law upon a book until they were finished]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 24:26: Καὶ ἔγραψε τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα εἰς βιβλίον νόμων τοῦ Θεοῦ [and he wrote these words in a book of laws of God]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/31/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: Deuteronomy says Moses wrote the words of the law in a book “until they were finished” and had it put beside the ark. Joshua then writes in a book with a like name. If it is the same book, something was written into the law after Moses; if it is another book, the passage speaks of a second writing that it does not describe. What “these words” covers — the covenant of that day, its statute and ordinance, or a longer account — is not said either, and it bears on what the passage claims about who wrote what.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verse states: that Joshua added a record of the Shechem covenant to the book Moses wrote; that “the book of the law of God” is a separate writing kept at the sanctuary; that “these words” are the statute and ordinance of verse 25 only; that the phrase points to the writing of the book of Joshua or of part of it. The record does not say that writing in the book would break any command. Brenton’s Greek as quoted has no article with “book” and has “laws” in the plural; that is noted and not examined. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV of Joshua for “book of the law” finds 1:8, 8:31, 8:34, 23:6 and 24:26, with “of Moses” at 8:31 and 23:6 and “of God” at 24:26 only; a search of the whole packaged KJV for “book of the law of God” finds Joshua 24:26 and Nehemiah 8:18, and Nehemiah 8:18 was not examined; Joshua 24:25–29 and Deuteronomy 31:24–26 were read in the KJV. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle which words Joshua wrote or in which book. A published record cites Deuteronomy 31:24–26 and Joshua 1:8 on the writing and keeping of the law, and another compares the place of the assembly in the Hebrew and the Greek; neither cites this question. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
